fake_negative_hypotheses: Calcium-based alloy catalysts can achieve enhanced efficiency and stability in electrochemical ammonia synthesis mediated by the nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) in non-aqueous systems due to their optimal bond strengths with hydroxides, which can be quantitatively evaluated using density functional theory (DFT) calculations and corroborated with in situ spectroscopy techniques during the electrocatalytic process.

Utilizing structured calcium metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) fabricated through solvothermal synthesis and tailored ligand design, as electrocatalysts for the nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) in non-aqueous systems, can enhance efficiency and stability. This enhancement will be achieved by optimizing both the pore structure and the functionalization of the MOFs to promote the ideal spatial arrangement of active sites. Such active sites will be designed to improve the interaction strength with nitrogen and hydroxide species under varied operational parameters—specifically pH levels between 7 and 12, temperatures from 25°C to 80°C, and electric potentials between -0.5V and -1.5V. The effectiveness of these modifications will be validated through in situ spectroscopy and electrochemical assessments, including cyclic voltammetry and chronoamperometry, coupled with theoretical predictions using density functional theory (DFT).

Developing structured calcium-based metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) with optimized hydroxide ion interaction features, tunable pore architectures, and tailored ligand designs can significantly enhance the efficiency and stability of the nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) for electrochemical ammonia synthesis in non-aqueous systems. This enhancement will arise from the deliberate modulation of bond strengths between calcium, nitrogen, and hydroxide species, evaluated through computational and experimental approaches, including density functional theory (DFT) and in situ spectroscopy. Specifically, this research will systematically investigate how variations in ligand compositions, pore structures, and electrochemical operational parameters (pH 7-12, temperatures of 25°C to 80°C, and electric potentials of -0.5V to -1.5V) impact the NRR's catalytic performance and provide a comparative analysis with existing lithium-based frameworks.

Calcium carbonate nanoparticles, utilized as catalysts in an optimized non-aqueous electrochemical system for ammonia synthesis, can mediate the nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) more effectively than lithium-based counterparts by adjusting hydroxide bond strengths through controlled synthesis methods and leveraging a forward osmosis-inspired strategy to enhance solute interactions. A systematic parametric study will investigate the influence of nanoparticle size, varying calcium concentrations, specific non-aqueous solvents, and precise electrochemical conditions (e.g., pH, temperature) on catalytic performance, with expected improvements in efficiency and stability leading to a more cost-effective ammonia production method.

By employing a specifically formulated calcium-cobalt alloy catalyst in a carbon-based non-aqueous electrolyte system, integrated with precisely synthesized palladium nanoparticles (2-5 nm in diameter) to enhance charge separation and minimize charge recombination, we can achieve a significant enhancement in the efficiency and stability of electrochemical ammonia synthesis via the nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR). This innovative approach is expected to yield ammonia with a Faradaic efficiency exceeding 60% while maintaining stability over 100 hours. The influence of bond strength interactions between calcium hydroxides and nitrogen species will be quantitatively evaluated through DFT calculations using the PBE functional with a double-zeta basis set. Additionally, performance metrics will be validated using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) while investigating the role of the carbon-based electrolyte's viscosity and conductivity for optimized reaction conditions.
gold_hypothesis: Calcium can mediate the electrochemical reduction of nitrogen to ammonia (Ca-NRR) in a non-aqueous system, utilizing calcium tetrakis(hexafluoroisopropyloxy)borate (Ca[B(hfip)4]2) or calcium borohydride (Ca(BH4)2) in tetrahydrofuran (THF) with a small amount of ethanol as a proton shuttle, achieving a Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 40 ± 2% for Ca[B(hfip)4]2 and 28 ± 3% for Ca(BH4)2.
model_negative_hypotheses: The electrochemical synthesis of ammonia can be efficiently mediated by a calcium-driven nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) in a non-aqueous system at room temperature. This innovative approach features a dual-function electrochemical cell that synergizes calcium plating/stripping with N<sub>2</sub> complexation, leveraging intentionally designed β-diketiminate ligands to enhance stabilization. Utilizing a calcium metal anode and a carbon-based cathode, the system operates within an organic electrolyte of Ca(BH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub> in tetrahydrofuran (THF), optimizing the reaction under a potential window of -0.5 to -2.5 V relative to a reference electrode. The incorporation of a specifically chosen co-substrate is proposed to preferentially stabilize calcium hydride side-products, thus enhancing the Faradaic efficiency to exceed 70% and surpass ammonia yields of existing lithium-based systems. In situ spectroscopic techniques, particularly in situ infrared spectroscopy and cyclic voltammetry, will be employed to comprehensively monitor reaction dynamics and mitigate side reactions, ensuring system stability over at least 150 cycles. The successful deployment of this system could pave the way for energy-efficient, cost-effective ammonia synthesis with significant implications for sustainable agriculture and the global chemical industry.

A calcium-mediated nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) for electrochemical ammonia synthesis can be achieved by utilizing low-valent calcium complexes in an electrochemical cell design that cycles calcium between Ca(0), Ca(I), and Ca(II) oxidation states. This process avoids external reductants like potassium by employing a cathode composed of nanostructured materials, such as graphene-decorated carbon nanotubes, which stabilize the calcium intermediates and facilitate efficient electron transfer. The cell operates using a non-aqueous electrolyte, such as tetrahydrofuran, under specific conditions with a potential range of -1.5V to -2.5V vs. a suitable reference electrode, enabling effective nitrogen adsorption and reduction.

Calcium-mediated nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) for electrochemical ammonia synthesis can be effectively realized by employing a dual-ligand system composed of a β-diketiminate ligand and an innovative phosphine-based secondary ligand to augment the electronic environment and stabilize low-valent calcium complexes. This system capitalizes on calcium’s capability to form a side-on bridging motif with dinitrogen. A simplified cyclical redox mechanism involving calcium cycling through Ca(I) and Ca(II) oxidation states will be executed within a uniquely engineered electrochemical cell. The cathode will consist of a multi-functional architecture of conductive polymers layered with nitrogen-doped graphene to optimize electron transfer and nitrogen adsorption. Utilizing a high solubility, non-aqueous electrolyte, such as tetrahydrofuran mixed with emerging superionic liquid co-solvents, the setup will ensure enhanced nitrogen solubility and ion conductivity. Optimal electrochemical conditions, especially a potential window from -1.3V to -1.8V vs. a standard electrode, will be employed to maximize the capture and reduction of N<sub>2</sub> and subsequent efficient hydrogenation. This approach aims to establish a sustainable, cost-effective, and high-efficiency alternative to lithium-based systems for ammonia synthesis.

Calcium can mediate the nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) for ammonia synthesis in a non-aqueous system at room temperature, utilizing an electrochemical cell with a calcium metal anode and a carbon-based cathode in an organic electrolyte such as Ca(BH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub> in tetrahydrofuran (THF). The system will operate under ambient pressure conditions, employing a potential range of -0.5 to -2.5 V relative to a reference electrode, aiming to achieve a Faradaic efficiency exceeding 50% and an ammonia yield rate comparable to or higher than that of lithium-based systems. Reaction conditions and potential side reactions will be monitored using in situ infrared spectroscopy and cyclic voltammetry to ensure stability and efficiency.

Calcium-mediated nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) for ammonia synthesis can be achieved with enhanced efficiency by utilizing a dual-electrolyte system that incorporates calcium plating and stripping via Ca(BH₄)₂ in tetrahydrofuran (THF) at the anode, while employing a proton-conducting polymer-based electrolyte at the cathode, such as Nafion™ or polybenzimidazole, optimized for nitrogen protonation and ammonia formation. This system will operate at room temperature in a nitrogen-saturated environment, benefiting from the interfacial dynamics of the dual-electrolyte system to notably increase Faradaic efficiency by at least 20% and ammonia yield rate compared to traditional lithium-based methodologies. Detailed electrochemical modeling and preliminary simulations will assess the feasibility and expected outcomes, addressing potential interface-related challenges.

Calcium complexes, facilitated by potassium as a terminal reductant, and utilizing specifically designed β-diketiminate ligands, can effectively mediate the nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) for electrochemical ammonia synthesis in non-aqueous systems. This process involves carefully selected ligands to stabilize the calcium complexes and optimized electrochemical conditions including electrode materials, cell design, temperature, pressure, and electrolyte composition to improve efficiency and stability over traditional lithium-based systems. Computational studies will guide ligand design and predict reaction pathways.

Calcium-mediated nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) for ammonia synthesis can be conducted in a novel dual-layer electrochemical cell utilizing an advanced MOF-enhanced carbon cathode and a layered hybrid electrolyte, operational at room temperature. This system will feature a calcium metal anode paired with a cathode composed of a specific nitrogen-permeable metal-organic framework (MOF), such as HKUST-1, embedded in a high-surface-area carbon matrix to maximize nitrogen adsorption and reduction efficiency. The electrolyte will comprise a layered configuration with Ca(BH₄)₂ in tetrahydrofuran (THF) for calcium ion transport, overlaid with a thin film of a proton-conducting ionic liquid, such as 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide (EMIM TFSI), optimized for proton transfer. The system will operate within a narrowed potential range of -0.7 to -2.5 V vs. a saturated calomel electrode (SCE), aiming for a minimum Faradaic efficiency of 65% and an ammonia yield surpassing that of lithium-based systems. Strategies will be incorporated to control calcium dendrite formation through thermal management and ionic electrolyte optimizations. In situ characterization methods, including Raman spectroscopy and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), alongside computational modeling, will facilitate real-time analysis of reaction pathways and system stability over extended operation. Comparisons of environmental and economic benefits of using calcium over lithium will be integral to the research's broader impact assessment.

Calcium can serve as a viable mediator for the nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) for ammonia synthesis in a non-aqueous system by forming stable calcium-dinitrogen coordination complexes utilizing specifically designed β-diketiminate ligands. By optimizing the concentration of calcium (0.1 M), ligands (0.05 M), and tetrabutylammonium tetrafluoroborate (TBABF₄) (0.5 M), and adjusting the N₂ pressure (1-5 atm) and temperature (room temperature, 25°C), we will establish a state-of-the-art three-electrode electrochemical cell. The protective layer formed by calcium hydride (CaH₂) during the plating process will not only stabilize the calcium but also enhance the electrochemical kinetics of NRR. The performance of this system will be quantitatively assessed against lithium-based systems through operando spectroscopy (using UV-Vis and FTIR to monitor the formation of calcium-dinitrogen complexes), gas chromatography for ammonia quantification, cyclic voltammetry for kinetic analysis, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy to evaluate stability and mass transport. The expected results will elucidate new mechanistic pathways for calcium-mediated NRR, demonstrating a significant enhancement in reaction rates and stability.

Calcium can mediate the nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) for ammonia synthesis in a non-aqueous system by forming tailored calcium-dinitrogen complexes, specifically LCa(N2)CaL, utilizing a diverse range of β-diketiminate ligands possessing distinct structural features that promote enhanced reactivity. This process can be optimized by rigorously controlling reaction parameters, including varying N2 pressures (up to 10 bar), temperatures (from 25 to 80 °C), and selecting non-aqueous solvents with high polarities, such as dimethylformamide and tetrahydrofuran. Furthermore, the introduction of nickel as a co-catalyst will occur in a 1:1 molar ratio to maximize electron transfer and coordination benefits. The efficiency and stability of this calcium-based approach will be quantitatively assessed through in situ operando spectroscopy and advanced electrochemical techniques, enabling real-time monitoring of performance metrics such as turnover frequency and selectivity for ammonia production against established lithium-based systems. Ultimately, this work aims to delineate the mechanistic pathways underlying N2 activation and reduction while establishing the broader significance of this method in advancing sustainable ammonia synthesis technologies.

Calcium can effectively mediate the nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) for ammonia synthesis in a non-aqueous electrolyte by leveraging its electrochemical properties and utilizing calcium hydride (CaH₂) as a protective layer. The hypothesis posits that a three-electrode electrochemical cell operating at room temperature with a carefully optimized tetrabutylammonium tetrafluoroborate (TBABF₄) electrolyte will enhance NRR efficiency. Characterization methods, including gas chromatography for ammonia quantification, cyclic voltammetry for kinetic assessment, and impedance spectroscopy for stability analysis, will be employed to evaluate the performance of Ca/CaH₂ systems against a lithium-based control catalyst, identifying key mechanistic pathways that facilitate NRR.
research_question: Can we develop a method for electrochemical ammonia synthesis that utilizes a more abundant and potentially more cost-effective metal than lithium, while maintaining comparable or better efficiency and stability? Specifically, can calcium mediate the nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) for ammonia synthesis in a non-aqueous system?
